title: Growth options and market share for a service business
audience: Owners and managers of service businesses who want to choose a growth option and need to know how much of their local market they hold.
referencesAtStart: Official source: business.gov.au, Guide to growing your business (page metadata date 09 January 2026; checked 2026-11-03). The Ansoff matrix and market share are standard planning concepts, explained here in new words. No market size figure is used in this lesson.
learningOutcomes: Place a growth option for a service business in one of the four Ansoff quadrants, by asking whether the service and the customer group are existing or new.
Calculate market share from a supplied sales figure and a supplied total market figure, and state whether the total is confirmed.
Choose one growth option, state its main risk, and name the measure that will show whether it works.

instruction.heading: The Ansoff matrix asks two questions
instruction.body: The Ansoff matrix is a planning grid for growth. It asks two questions: is the service you sell new or existing, and is the customer group you sell to new or existing? The answers place each growth option in one of four quadrants. The options carry different levels of risk, because a business knows more about some services and customers than others. Use the matrix to compare options before you spend money on one of them. It shows where the risk sits, but it does not decide the choice for you.

instruction.heading: Market penetration: existing service, existing customers
instruction.body: Market penetration means selling more of the service you already offer to the customer group you already serve. It is usually the lowest-risk option, because the business already knows the service and the customers. Ways to do it include more repeat bookings, a reminder system, a loyalty offer, or a stronger local presence. The limit is that a local market may already be well served, so growth can come only from taking clients from rivals or from clients using the service more often. Measure it with the number of repeat clients and the share of the market you hold, which is explained below.

instruction.heading: Market development and product development
instruction.body: Market development means selling an existing service to a new group of customers, such as households in a different suburb, a different type of property, or commercial clients instead of households. The business keeps the same service but must learn the new customers' needs, prices and buying habits. Product development means offering a new service to the customers you already serve, such as adding a related task to the same visit. This option uses the trust you have already built, but it needs new skills, equipment and pricing. Both options carry more risk than penetration, and each needs a test before the business commits to it. Before you test a new group, check your assumptions about it with research rather than guesswork. The Victorian Government's 'Who is my customer?' guidance suggests comparing how many competitors exist, how often buyers need the service and where they prefer to buy.

instruction.heading: Diversification: new service, new customers
instruction.body: Diversification has the highest risk, because both the service and the customer group are new. It can spread income across more than one kind of work, but the business is then learning two things at once. Consider it only when a simpler option has been tested and has reached its limit, or when a clear need exists and the business already has the skills to meet it. Treat a diversification as a separate project with its own costing, insurance check and review date, rather than as an add-on to the current work.

instruction.heading: Market share: the proportion you hold
instruction.body: Market share is the proportion of a market that one business controls. It is usually measured by sales revenue: your sales divided by the total sales of the market, written as a percentage. The calculation is simple, but the total market figure is often the hard part. A total may come from a survey, an industry report or an estimate, and each source has limits. Write the source and date of the total next to the share, and leave out the figure if you have not checked it. Read the share with the size of the market beside it. A share can rise even while your sales fall, if the whole market falls faster than you do.

instruction.heading: Choosing and measuring one option
instruction.body: Pick one growth option for the next period, not all four at once. Name its main risk, and the measure that will show whether it works, such as repeat bookings per month, or your share of the market in a named area. Set a review date, and decide in advance what result would mean stop and what would mean continue. Recording the decision in the business plan keeps the choice visible when the market changes.

procedure: Write the service you sell now and the customer group you serve now, in one line each.
For each of the four growth options, mark the service and the customer group as existing or new, and place the option in its quadrant.
For each option, list its main risk, the cost of testing it and the skills it needs.
Calculate market share from your sales and the total market sales for the same period, and write the source and date of the total.
Choose one option, set a measure and a review date, and decide in advance what result would mean stop and what would mean continue.

workedExamples.situation: EXAMPLE, invented for teaching and not market data: a small cleaning and maintenance business works mainly for households in one suburb. Its sales in the last year were $180,000. The total sales of the local market for the same year are not known, so for this example assume $1,200,000, marked as an assumption.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the market share, and which growth option should the owner test first?
workedExamples.reasoning: Market share is $180,000 divided by $1,200,000, which is 15 per cent in this example. Because the total is an assumption, the share is an example figure, not a fact about the real market. Next, place the options. Existing service for existing households is penetration. A commercial client for the same service is market development. A new related task added to the same visit is product development. The owner should test penetration first, for example by measuring repeat bookings over three months, because it has the lowest risk and uses existing skills. Set the review date and the stop-or-continue result before the test starts.

equipmentAndPpe: Sales records for the last full year, by month or by client group.
A written note of the total market figure, with its source and its date, and an estimate label if it is an estimate.
No personal protective equipment is needed for this desk-based lesson.

commonErrors.error: Treating an estimated market total as a fact.
commonErrors.prevention: Write the source and date next to the total, and label estimates as estimates.

commonErrors.error: Reading a rising market share as proof of growth while sales are falling.
commonErrors.prevention: Read the share with the size of the market and your sales for the same period.

commonErrors.error: Choosing diversification first because it sounds like the bigger move.
commonErrors.prevention: Test the lower-risk options first, unless a clear need and the skills are already in place.

commonErrors.error: Starting a test without a stop-or-continue result.
commonErrors.prevention: Set the measure, the review date and the stop-or-continue result before the test starts.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Growth into a new service or a new market may need a licence, a registration, a change to the insurance policy or a different contract. Licence and registration rules differ between states and territories, so check the rules where the new work will be done, and ask your insurer before you start.

Marketing to new customers must not mislead them. The ACCC's guidance on false or misleading claims says claims should be true, accurate and based on reasonable grounds. Electronic marketing needs consent and sender identification under ACMA's spam guidance. If the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) applies to your business, its privacy rules apply to new customer information too; check the OAIC's small business guidance to see whether it does.

qualityStandard: Each growth option is placed in its quadrant, with a reason for the placement.
The market share figure shows the sales used, the total market used, the period, and the source and date of the total.
One option is chosen with a measure, a review date and a stop-or-continue result.
documentationEvidence: Growth option sheet showing the four quadrants, the chosen option and its main risk.
Market share calculation with the source and date of each figure, and any estimate label.
summary: The Ansoff matrix sorts growth by whether the service and the customer group are existing or new.
Market share is your sales as a percentage of total market sales, and it is only as reliable as the total.
Test the lower-risk option first, with a measure and a stop-or-continue result set in advance.

knowledgeChecks.question: A service business already sells its work to households in one suburb and wants more of the same work there. Which growth option is this?
Which growth option means selling an existing service to a new group of customers?
In this example, your sales are $150,000 and the total market is $1,000,000 in the same year. What is your market share?
